title: Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) Access Model
date_evidence: CGT (Cell and Gene Therapy Access) Model | CMS — Number of State Participants: 34; Number of Manufacturer Participants: 2; Stage: Active (programme page, continuously updated)
key_claim: The CGT Access Model is the first time the federal government has negotiated outcomes-based agreements (OBAs) with cell and gene therapy manufacturers on behalf of state Medicaid agencies. It ties manufacturer payment to patient outcomes, with pricing discounts and outcomes-based rebates. The model now lists 34 state participants and 2 manufacturers (Vertex and Genetix Biotherapeutics); its initial focus is gene therapy for sickle cell disease, with states beginning participation between January 2025 and January 2026.
notes: Tier 1 government programme page (evergreen). Canonical description of the outcomes-based payment model that is the core of the signal.

title: Medicaid has a new way to pay for costly sickle cell treatment: Only if it works
date_evidence: Medicaid has a new way to pay for costly sickle cell treatment: Only if it works ... npr.org/2026/01/20/nx-s1-5682055
key_claim: The two FDA-approved sickle cell gene therapies cost $2.2 million and $3.1 million per patient (excluding the long hospital stay). Under the CMS model, participating states receive discounts and rebates if treatments do not work as promised; 33 states plus DC and Puerto Rico had joined, representing about 84% of Medicaid sickle cell patients. Clinical trials enrolled fewer than 100 patients with only two years of follow-up; uptake is low (Missouri: fewer than 10 of ~1,000 eligible enrollees treated so far). ICER's Sarah Emond calls it 'a worthy experiment' likely to be copied for other rare-disease therapies.
verbatim_quote: Medicaid has a new way to pay for costly sickle cell treatment: Only if it works
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band). Canonical narrative + pricing, utilisation and outcomes-based framing; also carries counter-evidence (patients benefiting, model being copied).

title: High-Stakes Medicine: Rethinking Policies for the Cost and Value of Cell and Gene Therapies
date_evidence: White Paper — March 19, 2026 — High-Stakes Medicine: Rethinking Policies for the Cost and Value of Cell and Gene Therapies
key_claim: The US system is built around chronic treatments paid over time and is poorly structured for one-time therapies whose value accrues over decades; CGTs combine very high up-front prices with long, uncertain benefit horizons, and diffusion has lagged expectations even for sickle cell disease. Provider reimbursement is an underappreciated barrier: hospitals often incur losses administering CGTs reimbursed below acquisition cost. The paper proposes a stepwise reform path: private-market intermediation first, then public-private hybrid models (akin to Medicare Part D), then direct public financing, with federal standardisation of longitudinal outcomes tracking.
notes: Tier 2 academic white paper; the structural diagnosis of why the one-time-cure payment model is mismatched, and the reform ladder.

title: Gene therapy brims with promise. The reality has been less rosy for some therapies (AMCP Annual 2026)
date_evidence: News | Videos | April 15, 2026 — Pfizer and BioMarin have pulled their hemophilia gene therapies, citing low demand.
key_claim: An even 20 gene therapies have been FDA-approved since Luxturna in December 2017. Uptake for several has fallen far short of forecasts: Pfizer pulled Beqvez (hemophilia B) in February 2025 and BioMarin is pulling Roctavian (hemophilia A), both citing limited demand. A common misconception is that all gene therapies are single-dose cures; some are multi-dose, adding complexity.
notes: Tier 3 trade press from AMCP Annual 2026; documents the commercial-uptake failures and withdrawals.

title: Sarepta Therapeutics Announces First Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Corporate Developments
date_evidence: CAMBRIDGE, Mass. -- (BUSINESS WIRE) -- May 6, 2026 -- Sarepta Therapeutics ... reported financial results for the first quarter 2026.
key_claim: ELEVIDYS, Sarepta's Duchenne gene therapy, generated $102.0 million in Q1 2026 net product revenue; its label was restricted to ambulatory patients only and it carries a boxed warning for acute serious liver injury and fatal acute liver failure after patient deaths. Sarepta announced a pipeline reprioritisation and restructuring in July 2025 and is pivoting toward siRNA programs, while stating its commercial portfolio 'has begun to stabilize.'
verbatim_quote: Our commercial portfolio has begun to stabilize
notes: Tier 1 primary filing (SEC 8-K exhibit). Illustrates safety-driven market narrowing of a flagship gene therapy and a pivot away; also supplies counter-evidence (stabilising).

title: Prime to test FDA flexibility with 2-patient gene editing submission
date_evidence: meta-date: 2026-03-04 ; Published March 4, 2026 — a year after Prime deprioritized the program for economic reasons
key_claim: Prime Medicine shelved its chronic granulomatous disease gene-editing therapy PM359 for economic reasons despite a promising two-patient result, because only about 50 US patients would be eligible, making the roughly $20-30 million development cost hard to balance against the market; the company has lost almost three-quarters of its value. BioPharma Dive frames this as 'a dilemma facing many makers of treatments for rare diseases,' compounded by a series of FDA gene therapy rejections and investor unease.
notes: Tier 3 quality trade journalism; the small-population commercial-viability dilemma and capital/regulatory pressure.

title: Gene Therapy — 2026 Market & Investment Trends
date_evidence: Gene Therapy - 2026 Market & Investments Trends - Tracxn (live sector dashboard, accessed June 2026)
key_claim: Through February 2026, gene therapy companies raised about $91.7 million in equity funding across 3 rounds, versus about $318 million across 9 rounds in the same period of 2025 - roughly a 71% year-on-year decline.
notes: Tier 4 commercial data vendor (live dashboard), used only as directional corroboration of the investment retreat.
